title: Building a Bridge from Noise to Terrain
concept_layer: coherent noise as randomness with spatial memory; gradient noise; octaves as self-similar detail
domain_deferred: simplex noise internals → later noise maps
fractal dimension of noise → fractals sequence

capture_leaks.two_dimensional_sampling: This uses 2D Perlin. The same function extends to 3D (volumetric clouds) and 4D (animated clouds). Volumetric noise deferred to procgen.
capture_leaks.gradient_vectors_hidden: Perlin computes noise from a grid of random gradient vectors. We see the output, not the gradients. Understanding the gradient dot product is what separates using noise from making noise.
capture_leaks.band_limited_signal: Perlin noise has no frequencies above ~2/grid_spacing. This is a feature (no aliasing) and a limit (fine detail needs octaves or different generator).
capture_leaks.deterministic_per_seed: Same seed + same coordinates = same output. The noise is reproducible — useful for procgen, but it also means Perlin noise is not random in the information-theoretic sense. It's compressed pseudo-randomness.
capture_leaks.no_large_scale_structure: Perlin noise is statistically homogeneous. If you want valleys and ridges at multiple scales, you sum octaves. Real terrain has tectonics — non-noise structure — that noise alone cannot give.

limit: Two grids: one chaos, one terrain. The only difference is whether neighbors remember each other. This is the essence of coherent noise. What it refuses: physical causality (noise doesn't know about erosion, plate tectonics, weather), time dependence (the field is static), and anisotropy (same behavior all directions). Real terrain is not noise; noise is a stand-in that often convinces us because our perception is statistical.

grammar_alignment.note: perlin_noise_bridge teaches perturb (displace each grid cell by noise sample) and terrain (use noise as height). The four noise operations are effectively: sample → displace → warp space itself → layer multiple scales. This artifact covers the first two side by side.

biome_alignment.note: Big moment — this is the first sequence where terrain_mode shifts from 'flat' to 'noise.' The biome no longer sits on a plane. Floors undulate. Vegetation follows the terrain. The player gains the 'sculpt_terrain' verb: they can push noise into the world and watch the ground respond.

stages.title: From entropy to memory
stages.thinking: Random_Definition taught that randomness dissolves order — each point independent, each offset fresh, entropy as a gradient. But nature doesn’t look like that. Mountains aren’t jittered grids. Clouds aren’t salt-and-pepper. Real landscapes have the statistical feel of randomness plus something else: neighbors influencing neighbors. That something is the subject of this map. What happens when randomness remembers?
stages.code:
# Random_Definition taught:
#   position += Vector3(
#     randf_range(-a, a),
#     randf_range(-a, a),
#     0
#   )
# Every point independent. Neighbors don't correlate.
#
# Now: what if position at (x, y) knew
# about position at (x-1, y)?
# What if randomness had a topology?
#
# This is the entire noise sequence in one question.

stages.title: Two grids side by side
stages.thinking: The teaching trick is juxtaposition. Build two 16×16 heightfield grids. Left grid: each cell's height is `randf()`. Right grid: each cell's height is `FastNoiseLite.get_noise_2d(x, y)`. Identical random range. Identical cell positions. Only difference: one is memoryless, the other isn't. Watching them side by side, the player feels why terrain looks like terrain.
stages.code:
extends Node3D
class_name PerlinNoiseBridge

const GRID_SIZE := 16
const CELL_WIDTH := 0.015
const MAX_HEIGHT := 0.15
const GRID_SPACING := 0.35  # distance between the two grids

var _noise: FastNoiseLite
var _white_columns: Array[MeshInstance3D] = []
var _perlin_columns: Array[MeshInstance3D] = []

func _ready() -> void:
	_noise = FastNoiseLite.new()
	_noise.noise_type = FastNoiseLite.TYPE_PERLIN
	_create_grids()
	_rebuild_grids()

stages.title: The left grid — pure randf()
stages.thinking: For each cell, pick a random height. No coordination with neighbors. This is the baseline — what randomness looks like without correlation. Every time you regenerate, it looks like static. Like TV between channels. Like salt on paper. The eye cannot find a pattern because there is no rule coupling neighbors.
stages.code:
func _rebuild_white_grid() -> void:
	for i in range(_white_columns.size()):
		var col = _white_columns[i]
		var h = randf() * MAX_HEIGHT  # each height independent
		col.mesh.size.y = max(0.001, h)
		col.position.y = h * 0.5

# Salt-and-pepper.
# Each call to randf() is a fresh draw.
# No memory. No structure. Pure noise.

stages.title: The right grid — FastNoiseLite.get_noise_2d()
stages.thinking: Same loop, same grid, same heightfield — but the height comes from a noise function that computes values from coordinates. Sample point (x, y). Its height correlates with the height at (x-1, y), (x, y-1), (x+1, y+1). Why? Because Perlin uses a grid of hidden gradient vectors, and the noise value at any point is a smooth blend of neighboring gradients. Neighbors are forced to agree. The output: hills, valleys, plausible landscape.
stages.code:
func _rebuild_perlin_grid() -> void:
	_noise.seed = _seed_val
	_noise.frequency = _frequency
	_noise.fractal_octaves = _octaves
	
	for i in range(_perlin_columns.size()):
		var col = _perlin_columns[i]
		var x = i % GRID_SIZE
		var y = i / GRID_SIZE
		
		# Sample noise at the grid coordinate
		# get_noise_2d returns [-1, 1]; remap to [0, MAX_HEIGHT]
		var n = _noise.get_noise_2d(float(x), float(y))
		var h = (n + 1.0) * 0.5 * MAX_HEIGHT
		
		col.mesh.size.y = max(0.001, h)
		col.position.y = h * 0.5

stages.title: Octaves — self-similar detail at every scale
stages.thinking: A single Perlin call produces rolling hills. But real terrain has hills on hills: big mountains with boulders with pebbles. Octaves solve this by summing multiple Perlin samples at increasing frequencies and decreasing amplitudes. Octave 1: big blobs, large amplitude. Octave 2: smaller blobs, half amplitude. Octave 3: finer still. Five octaves and you have something that looks like satellite imagery. FastNoiseLite sums them for you via fractal_octaves.
stages.code:
var _octaves: int = 3  # how many layers of detail
var _frequency: float = 2.0  # base frequency

_noise.fractal_octaves = _octaves
_noise.frequency = _frequency

# Internally, this computes:
#   total = 0
#   amplitude = 1
#   for i in octaves:
#     total += perlin(x * frequency, y * frequency) * amplitude
#     frequency *= 2.0      # next octave is twice as dense
#     amplitude *= 0.5       # and half as strong
#   normalize
#
# Self-similarity across scales.
# This is why octaves feel fractal.

stages.title: Seed, frequency, octaves — three sliders, infinite terrain
stages.thinking: Three parameters cover the entire Perlin parameter space for a terrain. Seed: reroll a new landscape with the same statistics. Frequency: change the scale of features (low = rolling, high = jagged). Octaves: how much fine detail. With these three sliders, the player can generate every plausible terrain. They also learn that terrain is a VALUE OF PARAMETERS — not a specific shape, but a region in parameter space.
stages.code:
func _create_vr_controls() -> void:
	var RackTpl = load("res://commons/audio/rack_templates/RackTemplates.gd")
	var panel = RackTpl.create_panel("PERLIN BRIDGE", [
		[{"type": "slider_h", "label": "OCTAVES", "default": _octaves / 8.0}],
		[{"type": "slider_h", "label": "FREQ", "default": _frequency / 10.0}],
		[{"type": "slider_h", "label": "SEED", "default": float(_seed_val) / 1000.0}],
		[{"type": "button", "label": "RESAMPLE"}],
	])

# Three sliders. Infinite distinct terrains.
# The player doesn't learn 'how to make terrain.'
# They learn that terrain is a region in a
# 3-dimensional parameter space.

stages.title: The rule-made coherence is visible
stages.thinking: Stand between the two grids. The white-noise grid shakes like TV snow. The Perlin grid breathes like a sleeping animal. The only difference is memory. This is what the bridge teaches without saying: coherence is not order imposed from above. It is the consequence of a rule that couples neighbors. Structure is free when the rule is right.
stages.code:
# The player stands between the two grids.
#
# LEFT:  randf()     — each cell lonely, no connection
# RIGHT: Perlin     — each cell whispers to its neighbors
#
# Same random [-1, 1] range.
# Same grid dimensions.
# Same update code.
#
# One looks like static. One looks like a place you could walk.
#
# No terrain rules were coded.
# No erosion was simulated.
# The rule was just: neighbors must agree a little.
#
# That's all it takes to move from chaos to landscape.

stages.title: Give it identity
stages.thinking: The bridge knows what it is. Not a terrain generator — a proof. The proof that when you add a neighbor-coupling rule to noise, terrain emerges for free. No tectonics, no erosion, no voxel carving. Just: ‘respect your neighbor.’ The critical parameter is frequency because it controls the scale of the feature — the deep variable that makes Perlin feel like a specific landscape. What the bridge refuses: real physics, large-scale structure, time evolution. All deferred, all earned later.
stages.code:
# @identity
# essence: Perlin(x,y) = smoothstep(dot(gradient, offset)) — gradient noise with spatial memory
# desire: see two grids side by side — one chaotic, one terrain — and feel the moment randomness becomes landscape
# critical_parameter: frequency — controls the scale of coherent features; low = rolling hills, high = jagged peaks
# triggers: _rebuild_grids() regenerates both heightfields when octaves, frequency, or seed change
# emerges: the Perlin grid looks like terrain not because terrain was coded, but because neighbors remember each other
# needs: FastNoiseLite [has]; RackTemplates panel with OCTAVES/FREQUENCY/SEED sliders [has]; RESAMPLE button [has]
# relationships: depends on white_noise_spectrum (conceptual base); feeds noise_layers and procedural terrain artifacts
# truth: Coherence is not the opposite of randomness — it is randomness with memory.
